name: a sunlit ridge near Shackleton crater, lunar South Pole
baseLabel: SUN-01 (fictional base placed at a real location)

nearbyComparisons.label: 300 m × 300 m area around the site (5×5 pixels, mean)

source.provider: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center — Planetary Geology, Geophysics and Geochemistry Lab (PGDA), LRO/LOLA team
source.product: AVGVISIB_85S_060M_201608 (Average solar illumination, 85°S–90°S, 60 m/px), PDS dataset LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0, product version V1.05
source.citation: Mazarico, E., Neumann, G.A., Smith, D.E., Zuber, M.T., Torrence, M.H. (2011). Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography. Icarus 211, 1066–1081. doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030
source.visualization: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, 'Illumination at the Moon's South Pole, 2023 to 2030' (ID 4930), https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4930

units: Dimensionless fraction 0–1: share of hourly time steps over an 18.6-year lunar nutation cycle in which the pixel was lit by any part of the solar disc. value = DN × 0.00004.
extraction: tools/extract-illumination.mjs: lat/lon converted to line/sample with the polar stereographic equations in DSMAP_POLAR.CAT (sphere 1737.4 km, 60 m/px, 5058×5058); only the needed image rows were read via HTTP Range requests. Map orientation was verified: five known permanently shadowed crater floors (Shackleton, Shoemaker, Faustini, Haworth, de Gerlache) read ≈0, while 3 of 4 longitude-mirrored control points read 0.17–0.35 (the 4th also fell in shadow). The site pixel equals the product's DERIVED_MAXIMUM (DN 22111), i.e. this pixel has the highest value in the map (ties possible).
limitations: Long-term average at the surface; panels on masts would see more sunlight.
'Sunlit' counts any visible fraction of the solar disc, so it is not the same as full panel output.
One 60 m pixel on a narrow ridge crest; the surrounding 300 m area averages much lower (0.55).
It is not a forecast for any specific date.
